title: Nehemiah 10:1–27
context: After the confession of chapter 9, the leaders set their seal to a written covenant. This unit keeps the list of signatories together: Nehemiah the governor, the priests (10:1–8), the Levites (10:9–13), and the chiefs of the people (10:14–27). Several names also appear in the returnee lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 and among the priestly houses of Nehemiah 12; some may stand for families rather than individuals, and those overlaps are noted without harmonizing. Versification: English 10:1–39 corresponds to Hebrew 10:2–40, and English 9:38 is Hebrew 10:1; this page follows the WEB numbering.

verses.text: Now those who sealed were: Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah,
verses.arminianNotes: The list of those who sealed begins with “Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah.” Arminian readers see leaders putting their own names first, freely binding themselves to the covenant they ask others to keep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see civil leadership heading the covenant renewal that follows the prayer of chapter 9. The identity of Zedekiah is not explained in the text, and readers in this tradition do not press any identification.

verses.arminianNotes: Seraiah, Azariah, and Jeremiah head the priestly signatories. Arminian readers see priests publicly committing themselves to the law they were called to teach and uphold among the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priesthood taking responsibility in the renewal. Several of these names also appear among the priestly houses in Nehemiah 12:1–21, and they may represent families rather than single individuals.

verses.arminianNotes: Pashhur, Amariah, and Malchijah continue the priestly list. Arminian readers see each name recorded as a personal commitment, so that the covenant is not merely an abstract national promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful record honoring those who bound themselves to God’s law. The Pashhur family also appears in the returnee lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7.

verses.arminianNotes: Hattush, Shebaniah, and Malluch are added. Arminian readers see a broad priestly participation, with many households joining the leaders in a public pledge of obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the breadth of the priestly commitment. Readers in this tradition treat the overlap of names with other lists in Ezra and Nehemiah cautiously, since similar names recur across generations.

verses.arminianNotes: Harim, Meremoth, and Obadiah are listed. Arminian readers see families with histories in the return now renewing their commitment to walk in God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity between the returnees and this covenant. Harim and Meremoth appear elsewhere in Ezra–Nehemiah, though readers in this tradition do not assume every occurrence refers to the same person.

verses.arminianNotes: Daniel, Ginnethon, and Baruch continue the list. Arminian readers see that the names of ordinary priests are preserved, reflecting the value of each person’s commitment before God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the record dignifying faithful servants. These names are not to be identified with better-known figures who bore them, such as the prophet Daniel or Jeremiah’s scribe Baruch.

verses.arminianNotes: Meshullam, Abijah, and Mijamin are named. Arminian readers see the priestly community joining together, each family freely accepting its share of responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the united commitment of the priesthood. Abijah and Mijamin also appear among the priestly houses in Nehemiah 12, reflecting the family structure of the priesthood.

verses.text: Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah. These were the priests.
verses.arminianNotes: Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah close the list: “These were the priests.” Arminian readers see the priestly section completed, with leaders publicly accountable for keeping the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priests’ part in the renewal recorded in full. The closing formula marks the transition to the Levites, preserving the order of the community’s leadership.

verses.text: The Levites: Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites begin with Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui, and Kadmiel. Arminian readers see those who assisted in teaching the law now binding themselves to it as well.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Levites joining the covenant. Jeshua, Binnui, and Kadmiel are Levitical names found elsewhere in Ezra–Nehemiah, and readers in this tradition hold precise identifications loosely.

verses.text: and their brothers, Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
verses.arminianNotes: Their brothers Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, and Hanan follow. Arminian readers see that several of these names appear among the Levites who helped the people understand the law in Nehemiah 8:7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a link with the teaching of the law in chapter 8. Those who explained God’s word now commit themselves publicly to obey it, joining instruction to practice.

verses.arminianNotes: Mica, Rehob, and Hashabiah are added. Arminian readers see the Levitical community broadly represented, each household accepting its responsibility under the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful naming of the Levites. The list shows that the renewal involved the whole range of temple servants, not only the most prominent leaders.

verses.arminianNotes: Zaccur, Sherebiah, and Shebaniah continue the list. Arminian readers note that Sherebiah also appears among the teachers of the law in Nehemiah 8:7, showing continuity between instruction and commitment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the same Levitical names recurring in the reading of the law and the covenant. The repetition of Shebaniah may reflect two different persons, which readers in this tradition leave open.

verses.arminianNotes: Hodiah, Bani, and Beninu close the Levites. Arminian readers see the Levitical section completed, showing a community of teachers and servants united in renewed obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Levites’ commitment recorded in full. A second Hodiah in the list may indicate a different person, and the text does not explain the repetition.

verses.text: The chiefs of the people: Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Zattu, Bani,
verses.arminianNotes: The chiefs of the people begin with Parosh, Pahathmoab, Elam, Zattu, and Bani. Arminian readers see lay leaders joining the priests and Levites, so the whole community is represented.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see family heads committing their households. Several of these names match family groups in the returnee lists of Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, suggesting that some entries represent clans rather than individuals.

verses.arminianNotes: Bunni, Azgad, and Bebai are listed. Arminian readers see families that had returned from exile renewing their commitment to live by God’s law in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity with the returnee lists, where Azgad and Bebai also appear. Readers in this tradition note the overlap without assuming that every name corresponds exactly.

verses.arminianNotes: Adonijah, Bigvai, and Adin follow. Arminian readers see lay households publicly accepting the obligations of the covenant along with the religious leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people’s leaders joining the pledge. Bigvai and Adin appear in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, and some suggest Adonijah corresponds to a similar name there, though this is uncertain.

verses.arminianNotes: Ater, Hezekiah, and Azzur are named. Arminian readers see family heads taking personal responsibility for leading their households in obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant embraced by many families. The names Ater and Hezekiah are linked in the returnee lists of Ezra 2:16 and Nehemiah 7:21, though here they appear separately.

verses.arminianNotes: Hodiah, Hashum, and Bezai continue. Arminian readers see a growing list that shows the breadth of the community’s commitment to God’s law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful record of each household. Hashum and Bezai appear among the returnee families, reinforcing the link between the return and this renewal.

verses.arminianNotes: Hariph, Anathoth, and Nobai are listed. Arminian readers note that Anathoth is also a town name, and here it may represent people associated with that place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see that some names may stand for families or towns rather than individuals. Readers in this tradition hold such identifications tentatively, as the text does not explain them.

verses.arminianNotes: Magpiash, Meshullam, and Hezir follow. Arminian readers see further households binding themselves to the covenant, each contributing to a shared commitment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people’s leaders committing themselves to God’s law. The list reflects a community taking ownership of its obedience after the confession of chapter 9.

verses.arminianNotes: Meshezabel, Zadok, and Jaddua are listed. Arminian readers see each name as a public witness to a freely made pledge before God and the community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant embraced by a wide range of leaders. These names are not to be confused with priests of the same names mentioned elsewhere.

verses.arminianNotes: Pelatiah, Hanan, and Anaiah follow. Arminian readers see the community’s commitment spreading through many families, not resting only on a few leaders.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the breadth of the covenant renewal. Readers in this tradition value the reminder that God’s people are made up of many households, each accountable to him.

verses.arminianNotes: Hoshea, Hananiah, and Hasshub are named. Arminian readers see further households joining the pledge, showing broad participation in the renewal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful naming of each household. The list continues the pattern of recording lay leaders who committed themselves to walk in God’s law.

verses.arminianNotes: Hallohesh, Pilha, and Shobek are listed. Arminian readers note that the name Hallohesh also appears in Nehemiah 3:12, in the family of a wall builder, which may suggest continuity between rebuilding and renewal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the possible connection with the wall builders. Readers in this tradition hold the identification loosely while appreciating the link between physical and spiritual restoration.

verses.arminianNotes: Rehum, Hashabnah, and Maaseiah follow. Arminian readers see the list nearing completion, with many families publicly accountable to the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the community’s leaders recorded. The repeated pattern of names shows the seriousness with which the renewal was documented.

verses.arminianNotes: Ahiah, Hanan, and Anan are named. Arminian readers see the commitment continuing through the final households of the list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the careful record nearing its end. A second Hanan in this list may represent a different person, and readers in this tradition leave the question open.

verses.arminianNotes: Malluch, Harim, and Baanah close the list. Arminian readers see the full roster of leaders completed, preparing for the description of the oath taken by all the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the list of signatories concluded. The repetition of names such as Malluch and Harim from the priestly list likely reflects common family names rather than the same individuals.
